summary.text: The form is unchanged in representability when the two square terms are exchanged, so representability for (1,2,1,1) implies representability for (2,1,1,1) by swapping x and y. The proposed classification contains the former quadruple but omits the latter, contradicting its claimed equivalence.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
P(a,b,c,d)
\]
denote the assertion that \(a,b,c,d\) are positive integers and that every nonnegative integer \(n\) has a representation
\[
n=ax^2+by^2+cz^3+dw^4
\]
with \(x,y,z,w\) nonnegative integers. Let \(S\) be the displayed set of 49 quadruples in the conjecture.

The key observation is that full representability is symmetric in the first two coefficients. More precisely, for all positive integers \(a,b,c,d\),
\[
P(a,b,c,d)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad P(b,a,c,d).
\]
Indeed, suppose first that \(P(a,b,c,d)\) holds. The coefficients \(b,a,c,d\) are still positive. Given any nonnegative integer \(n\), choose nonnegative integers \(x,y,z,w\) such that
\[
n=ax^2+by^2+cz^3+dw^4.
\]
Set
\[
X=y,\qquad Y=x,\qquad Z=z,\qquad W=w.
\]
Then all four new variables are nonnegative, and by commutativity of addition,
\[
\begin{aligned}
bX^2+aY^2+cZ^3+dW^4
 &=by^2+ax^2+cz^3+dw^4\\
 &=ax^2+by^2+cz^3+dw^4\\
 &=n.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus every nonnegative \(n\) is represented with coefficients \((b,a,c,d)\), proving \(P(b,a,c,d)\). Applying the same argument a second time, or simply interchanging \(a\) and \(b\), proves the converse. Hence the claimed symmetry follows.

Now assume, for contradiction, the conjectured classification:
\[
P(a,b,c,d)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad (a,b,c,d)\in S
\]
for every quadruple of nonnegative integers \((a,b,c,d)\) (with positivity already included in the definition of \(P\)).

The quadruple
\[
(1,2,1,1)
\]
appears explicitly as the first member of the displayed set \(S\). Therefore
\[
(1,2,1,1)\in S.
\]
Using the right-to-left implication of the assumed classification, it follows that
\[
P(1,2,1,1)
\]
holds. In expanded form, this says that the four coefficients are positive and that, for every nonnegative integer \(n\), there are nonnegative integers \(x,y,z,w\) satisfying
\[
n=x^2+2y^2+z^3+w^4.
\]

By the symmetry of the two square terms established above, \(P(1,2,1,1)\) implies
\[
P(2,1,1,1).
\]
Concretely, if
\[
n=x^2+2y^2+z^3+w^4,
\]
then, after exchanging the two square variables, one has
\[
n=2y^2+x^2+z^3+w^4.
\]
Thus a representation for the coefficient quadruple \((1,2,1,1)\) gives a representation for the coefficient quadruple \((2,1,1,1)\), for every \(n\). The new coefficients \(2,1,1,1\) are all positive, so this proves the full property \(P(2,1,1,1)\), including its positivity requirement.

Applying the left-to-right implication of the assumed classification to this conclusion yields
\[
(2,1,1,1)\in S.
\]
But this is false by direct inspection of the displayed finite list. To make the check explicit, the only listed quadruples whose first coordinate is \(2\) are
\[
(2,3,1,1),\quad (2,4,1,1),\quad (2,4,1,2),\quad
(2,3,1,4),\quad (2,3,1,5),\quad (2,4,1,5),\quad
(2,4,1,11).
\]
Every one of these has second coordinate \(3\) or \(4\), never \(1\). Hence
\[
(2,1,1,1)\notin S,
\]
contradicting the membership forced by the conjectured equivalence.

Therefore it is not true that, for every quadruple \((a,b,c,d)\), the form \(ax^2+by^2+cz^3+dw^4\) is fully representative exactly when \((a,b,c,d)\) belongs to the stated list. The list fails to respect the unavoidable symmetry obtained by exchanging the two square terms, so the conjecture is false.
